fields.Back: the set of all linear combinations \(\alpha_1v_1+\dots+\alpha_nv_n\), with \(\alpha_i\in\mathbb R\)
fields.SpeakFront: the span of v one through v n
fields.SpeakBack: the set of all linear combinations, alpha one v one plus through alpha n v n, with real alphas
fields.Elaboration: The span is always a subspace. The vectors form a spanning set for \(S\) if their span equals \(S\).

fields.Back: \(\alpha_1v_1+\dots+\alpha_kv_k=0\implies\alpha_1=\dots=\alpha_k=0\): the only combination giving the zero vector is the trivial one
fields.SpeakFront: v one through v k are linearly independent if and only if what?
fields.SpeakBack: the only linear combination that gives the zero vector is the one with every coefficient zero
fields.Elaboration: Dependent means some vector is a combination of the others.

fields.Front: A single vector \(v\) is linearly dependent iff…
fields.SpeakFront: a single vector v is linearly dependent if and only if what?
fields.Elaboration: \(1\cdot\mathbf 0=\mathbf 0\) is a nontrivial combination. So any set containing \(\mathbf 0\) is dependent.

golden.note: The student highlighted it, so it counts as emphasis.

fields.Front: \(n\) vectors in \(\mathbb R^n\) are linearly dependent iff the matrix \(X=[x_1\ \cdots\ x_n]\) is…
fields.SpeakFront: n vectors in R n are linearly dependent if and only if the matrix with those columns is what?
fields.Elaboration: A square matrix only. For \(m\ne n\), row-reduce instead.

golden.note: 'n vectors in ℝⁿ' in the prompt is the precision cue (canon 2).

fields.Front: If a square matrix \(A\) has linearly dependent rows, must its columns be dependent? Why?
fields.Back: Yes: \(\det A^T=\det A\), so \(\det A=0\) either way
fields.SpeakFront: if a square matrix has linearly dependent rows, must its columns be dependent too? Why?
fields.SpeakBack: yes, because the determinant of A transpose equals the determinant of A, so both are zero
fields.Elaboration: Row rank = column rank, for any matrix.

golden.note: Answers 'does det(Aᵀ) = det(A)?' inside the true/false item it came from.

fields.Back: a set of vectors that is linearly independent and spans \(V\)
fields.SpeakFront: definition of a basis of a vector space V
fields.SpeakBack: a set of vectors that is linearly independent and spans V
fields.Elaboration: Spanning means enough vectors; independent means none extra.

fields.Front: Why does a basis give each vector a unique set of coordinates?
fields.Back: If \(v=\sum a_iv_i=\sum b_iv_i\), then \(\sum(a_i-b_i)v_i=0\), and independence forces \(a_i=b_i\)
fields.SpeakFront: why does a basis give each vector a unique set of coordinates?
fields.SpeakBack: if v has two expansions, subtracting gives a combination equal to zero, and independence forces every coefficient difference to be zero
fields.Elaboration: Spanning gives existence; independence gives uniqueness.

golden.note: The student's own handwritten proof becomes the answer: cards reinforce derivations he already did.

fields.Front: Dimension of \(\mathbb R^{2\times2}\), the space of 2×2 real matrices
fields.SpeakFront: dimension of the space of two by two real matrices
fields.SpeakBack: four; one basis matrix for each entry
fields.Elaboration: Each matrix has 4 independent entries, so the space looks like \(\mathbb R^4\), not \(\mathbb R^2\). \(\{e_1,e_2\}\) can't produce a 2×2 matrix.

golden.note: Answers 'is this not just 2D?'. Tagged type::trap because the error is intuitive.

fields.Situation: Trimming a spanning set down to a basis by row reduction
fields.Trap: Taking the columns of the REF/RREF as the basis vectors
fields.Fix: Use the columns of the original matrix \(A\) at the pivot positions
fields.Why: Row operations change the column space; they only preserve which columns are independent.
fields.SpeakSituation: trimming a spanning set down to a basis by row reduction
fields.SpeakFix: use the original matrix's columns at the pivot positions, not the reduced matrix's columns

golden.note: The red 'from REF?' is exactly the classic mistake.

fields.Front: If \(\{v_1,\dots,v_n\}\) spans \(V\), what's true of any \(k>n\) vectors in \(V\)?
fields.SpeakFront: if n vectors span V, what is true of any collection of more than n vectors in V?
fields.Elaboration: So every basis has the same size, which is what makes dimension well defined. For an \(n\times(n+1)\) matrix: \(n+1\) columns in \(\mathbb R^n\) are always dependent.

golden.note: The corollary (every basis has the same size) goes in Elaboration, which also answers the red 'proof?'.

fields.Situation: Deciding whether two vectors in \(\mathbb R^2\) or \(\mathbb R^3\) are linearly independent
fields.Fix: Independent just means not parallel: neither is a multiple of the other. \((1,1)\) and \((1,2)\) are independent but not orthogonal.
fields.Why: Orthogonal nonzero vectors are always independent, but not the other way round. In \(\mathbb R^3\), \(\lVert v_1\times v_2\rVert\ne0\) is exactly the test for two vectors.
fields.SpeakSituation: deciding whether two vectors in the plane or in space are linearly independent
fields.SpeakFix: independent just means not parallel; one and one, and one and two, are independent but not orthogonal

golden.note: The student's question gets both answers: orthogonality, no; cross product, yes.
